title: PwC UK: eVTOL aircraft unlikely to replace cars or trains - Dronewatch Europe
text: PwC UK: eVTOL aircraft unlikely to replace cars or trains - Dronewatch Europe Skip to content Sunday, November 15, 2026 Drone delivery Industry Market Regulations Business Directory Vacancies List your vacancy with us Newsletter About us Advertise on Dronewatch Contact us Privacy policy Urban Air Mobility PwC UK: eVTOL aircraft unlikely to replace cars or trains August 12, 2026 Wiebe de Jager 0 Comments eVTOL , United Kingdom Share Tweet Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOLs), often described as “flying taxis”, are unlikely to play a significant role in the UK as an alternative to cars and trains. That is the conclusion of a new PwC UK study , which uses a year of anonymised travel data to assess which existing transport routes could realistically be served by eVTOLs. Even under highly favourable assumptions, the number of viable routes turns out to be very limited. No viable routes at 5% adoption For the study, PwC built on its 2023 research into Advanced Air Mobility in the UK. The new analysis uses anonymised and aggregated travel data from BT as a proxy for actual journeys. Geospatial analysis was then used to assess, route by route, whether passengers could theoretically switch from cars or trains to eVTOL aircraft. At the maximum adoption assumption used in the earlier study – 5% by 2040 – PwC finds zero viable routes. Only at an adoption rate of 17% does a single route become viable for an eVTOL service in economic and practical terms. Even at an intentionally unrealistic 100% adoption rate, the model identifies only 205 routes on which eVTOLs could provide a viable alternative. Combined, these routes account for just 0.05% of all weekly person-trips in the UK. Model stacked in favour of eVTOL The findings are particularly striking because PwC has made several assumptions that favour eVTOL. The analysis uses optimistic aircraft costs, ideally located vertiports and short walking distances to and from those vertiports. The impact of weather and limited aircraft utilisation is also relatively constrained. The model further assumes balanced demand in both directions, high average passenger occupancy and no so-called deadheading – empty return flights after passengers have been dropped off. Barriers such as public perception, infrastructure and regulation are also excluded from the calculation. In reality, these factors could make the introduction of eVTOL services even more difficult. No allowance for new demand There is, however, an important caveat to the analysis. PwC only looks at substitution: whether existing journeys by car or train could be replaced by eVTOLs. The model does not account for additional transport demand that could be generated by the availability of a new form of air mobility. This means, for example, that people who do not currently travel, or who make much longer journeys because a direct connection is unavailable, are not included in the analysis. PwC therefore cautions that the study should not be interpreted as evidence that eVTOLs cannot generate new mobility demand. Room for niche applications The researchers do see opportunities for specific, geographically limited applications. These could include replacing conventional helicopter services, selected premium connections and routes where direct long-distance connectivity offers a clear advantage. In other words, eVTOLs could become part of the UK’s transport system, but probably not as a flying replacement for existing public transport. The technology appears better suited to a limited number of specific connections. Significant barriers remain The study also revisits the main obstacles to the development of Advanced Air Mobility. PwC identifies public acceptance, infrastructure, safety and security, technological development, regulation, skills and viable business models as key challenges. There has been progress in some of these areas since the previous study in 2023. However, PwC concludes that the fundamental barriers to large-scale adoption remain significant. In some areas, the challenges now appear even greater than they did three years ago. A reality check on earlier expectations PwC’s conclusions inevitably bring to mind the high expectations of less than seven years ago. At the first edition of Amsterdam Drone Week in 2019, there was already considerable discussion about a future in which air taxis would transform urban transport. In a retrospective published at the time, Dronewatch noted the striking gap between the futuristic presentations about Urban Air Mobility and the much more mundane problems involved in operating small drones. That gap has arguably become even more visible since then. Two of the best-known European eVTOL pioneers of that era, Lilium and Volocopter, ran into serious financial trouble in 2024 and entered insolvency proceedings. Lilium subsequently failed to sustain its operations, while Volocopter eventually pursued a different path following a restart. Perhaps the air taxis envisioned in 2019 were not simply too early for the market – but too early for the expectations that had been built around them.
